string-array.name: help_texts
string-array.item: Scrambled Net 2 is a simple puzzle game in which you sort out the connections in a computer network, so that all the terminals are connected to the server. The network is made up of tiles; they are all in the right place, but they have been randomly rotated into a useless mess.\n\nRotate individual tiles to re-connect the network. Tiles connected to the server are shown highlighted. When every terminal is connected, you win.

Touch a tile to rotate it clockwise. Press and hold a tile to lock it when you are sure it is correct, or to unlock it; locked tiles answer with a short click.\n\nDrag with one finger to pan the board, pinch with two fingers to zoom.

There are five levels of difficulty. Higher levels have larger boards, and the most advanced have special twists:

• Novice: a small board.

• Normal: a somewhat larger board.

• Expert: a large board.

• Master: a large board whose edges wrap around — a connection leaving the right edge enters the left edge, and likewise for the top and bottom edges.

• Insane: like Master, but all 3-way and 4-way tiles are invisible. You will need a whole new set of deductions to complete an insane puzzle.

Each win counts your moves and your time, and your personal bests are kept for every skill level — but only if you solved the puzzle yourself: a game in which the auto-solver was used is never scored.\n\nSee “High scores” in the menu.

Work outwards from the server: confirmed tiles are your anchors, so lock them in as you go.

Tiles with a single connection are terminals — dead ends; aim them at the neighbour that needs them.

If you prefer a quiet board, you can switch the network animation off in the menu.

string-array.name: about_texts
string-array.item: Scrambled Net 2 is a modern, open-source remake of Scrambled Net, an Android port of the KDE game KNetWalk. Untangle a scrambled computer network so that every terminal is connected to the server: all the tiles are in the right place, but randomly rotated. Rotate them one by one to rebuild the network.

Scrambled Net 2 is the work of Éric Chardon, a lifelong enthusiast of logic and puzzle games. In early 2010 he discovered Ian Cameron Smith\'s famous application, shipped with its source code, and in 2014 its takeover by Michael Mueller — expecting the latter to bring more evolutions to the game and keep players interested. As the years went by without those hopes materializing, he decided to write the awaited sequel himself: this modern, open-source remake, faithful to the original.

KNetWalk, the original KDE game: © 2004–2007 Andi Peredri, Thomas Nagy and Fela Winkelmolen.

 Scrambled Net, the Android port: © 2007–2010 Ian Cameron Smith, © 2014 Michael Mueller.

This remake, Scrambled Net 2: © 2026 Éric Chardon.

 All distributed under the GPL-2.0 license — this game is free software.

Source code: https://github.com/echardon69-collab/Scrambled-Net-2

You can help improve the game:

• Report a bug — link to come.

• Contact the author — link to come.

• Propose a translation into a new language — link to come.

• Propose a new tile skin — link to come.

Compared with the original game, this remake adds:

• The Endless family: three new skill levels (Endless, Abyss, Void) on a giant 40 × 40 board whose edges wrap around — the camera loops on itself, panning never shows an edge; Abyss hides the wiring, Void adds fog over the network.

• A title screen with automatic updates from GitHub, in two distribution flavours: the GitHub APK with the built-in updater, the Play Store APK without it.

• An electricity signature: the server lights and the data blips pulse with a different rhythm depending on which generator built the board.

• The description of every skill level — real board size and rules — in the Settings page.

• A language setting (English, French, or follow the system).

Features the original had, now done differently:

• Source code: Java and Ant have been replaced by Kotlin and Gradle.

• Graphics: the bitmaps of the original are now VectorDrawables — same look, perfectly sharp at any zoom, one file for every screen density.

• Sound: no sample from the original is reused; six short effects are synthesized instead.

• Rendering: instead of a constant animation loop, the board redraws only when something changes — easier on the battery.

• The board no longer stretches to fill the screen: it is a camera viewport you can drag and zoom with your fingers, and the zoom stays anchored under them.

• Board generation: half the boards come from an alternate spanning-tree generator that connects every cell (the original generator still builds the other half — the electricity signature tells them apart).

• Menus: a text action bar without title, settings on a single page instead of cascading submenus, and the About dialog became this page.

Features of the original, kept as they were:

• The five original skill levels (Novice to Insane) with their exact rules — Master's wrapping edges, Insane's hidden wiring.

• The original board generator: every puzzle can be won, and the game is won when every terminal is connected.

• Board sizes adapt to your screen and orientation, exactly as the original's Screen matrix did.

• Touch a tile to rotate it, press and hold to lock or unlock it.

• The auto-solver — a solved game is never scored.

• Personal bests (moves and time) for each skill level.

• The saved game survives closing the app or letting it sleep; the clock freezes in the background.

• The rules reminders when entering Master or Insane.

• The three sound modes and the animation setting.

• The in-game help.

Features of the original that are gone, and why:

• The D-pad, trackball and keyboard controls: this remake is touch-only, built for modern phones and tablets.

• The persistent red focus cursor, designed for the D-pad era: with direct touch it was noise rather than help — the alert blink and the auto-solver's moving cursor cover what it was for.

• Every dependency of the original (the HermitAndroid and HermitLibrary libraries, including the MTRandom random generator, replaced by Kotlin's standard generator): the engine was rewritten from scratch in Kotlin as a pure, unit-tested game engine — no code from the original is reused.
